newsitem.title: USA: Dollar holds onto gains to close near U.S. highs.
newsitem.headline: Dollar holds onto gains to close near U.S. highs.

text.p: The dollar reversed a series of losses against the yen and mark to close higher, fueled by pro-dollar statements from Bundesbank officials, traders said.

The dollar began its climb after Bundesbank council member Edgar Meister said the current dollar/mark rate below 1.50 marks was not appropriate, echoing earlier comments from fellow council member Hans-Juergen Krupp that a firmer dollar might seem more appropriate.
But dealers remained somewhat skeptical of renewed dollar strength until Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the dollar was on its way back up, a move he welcomed.
"People waited for Tietmeyer to speak to see if he would add any credibility to the earlier Bundesbank comments," said Bob Houck, vice president at Norwest Bank in Minneapolis.
"Once he collaborated, short (sellers) started covering their positions and the bulls jumped on board," he added.

The dollar shot higher after Tietmeyer spoke to hit an intraday high of 1.5090 marks. It closed slighly below the high at 1.5070/75 marks, compared to 1.4980/90 at Tuesday's open. The dollar also gained to 1.2680/90 Swiss francs, up from 1.2595/05 Swiss francs at the open.
However, the concern failed to translate into significant mark buying. The mark is typically viewed as a currency safe-haven if EMU were to begin to unravel, dealers said.

"It appears Germany will take a tact, even if they are tough on the EMU criteria, of trying to keep the dollar stable," said Mark Gargano, managing director of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank in Charlotte, North Carolina.
The Bundesbank comments overshadowed remarks last week from key Japanese officials which raised concerns Japan might be changing its longstanding strong-dollar, weak-yen policy.
The dollar gained to close at 111.45/50 yen, up from 111.25/35 at Tuesday's open, after falling for four consecutive U.S. sessions.

Many dealers expressed doubt that yen weakness against the dollar has come to an end, as Japanese officials previously stated, due to the large interest rate differential between the United States and Japan.
"Japan doesn't want dollar/yen going higher, but they also want to keep their rates down, so I don't think anyone buys it," Gargano said.
Dealers also cited market talk that President Bill Clinton could make significant headway towards a balanced U.S. budget over the next few months as helping the dollar.
The dollar also fell to Canadian $1.3323/28 from C$1.3340/45 at Tuesday's open. The Australian dollar ended at $0.7870/75, unchanged from the open.
